name: Ingot-Depths
geological_features: Geothermal vent fields on the abyssal floor
Submerged mountain ranges rising to within meters of the surface
Perpetual storm systems driven by thermal differentials
specific_features: Sunken colony ship serving as artificial reef
Research outpost built on a stabilized platform
description: Ingot-Depths is a world of unbroken ocean, its surface a restless expanse of dark, mineral-heavy water that gleams like liquid metal under the light of its binary suns. No land breaks the horizon in any direction; the only relief comes from shallow regions where submerged mountain peaks create lighter patches of turquoise amid the prevailing iron-grey. Massive storm systems patrol the equatorial belt, their lightning illuminating waters that plunge to depths of over forty kilometers.

The dense atmosphere presses down like a physical weight, and the air is thick with salt and the ozone tang of constant electrical discharge. The ocean's surface heaves with slow, powerful swells that can reach thirty meters in height during storm season, making surface operations a constant negotiation with the elements. At dawn, the binary suns create two overlapping sets of reflections that shatter across the waves in patterns of breathtaking complexity.

A colony ship, the MV Ingot Star, crash-landed in the shallows three centuries ago and has since become the nucleus of a thriving artificial reef ecosystem. The ship's hull, partially exposed above the waterline, serves as the foundation for the only permanent structure on the planet. Its original colonists were bound for a terrestrial world and were wholly unprepared for an oceanic existence, but their descendants have adapted, becoming expert aquaculturists and deep-sea harvesters.

The abyssal trenches remain largely unexplored, and deep-submersible expeditions have returned with reports of bioluminescent megafauna unlike anything in the catalogued xenobiological record. The geothermal vents on the ocean floor produce concentrations of helium-3 that would be enormously valuable if extraction were feasible. Recent sonar mapping has revealed geometric patterns on the deepest seabed that may be natural formations or may be something else entirely.
